subject: Chemistry
title: Sarin: The Nerve Agent
description: A 60-second lesson on Sarin: The Nerve Agent.

hook.text: Sarin is 500 times more toxic than cyanide. A single drop on skin can kill in minutes.

buildup.text: Developed in 1938 by German scientists trying to make stronger pesticides, sarin was classified as a weapon of war.

discovery.text: Sarin blocks acetylcholinesterase—the enzyme that turns off nerve signals. Without it, muscles fire nonstop.

twist.text: Every muscle contracts simultaneously: pupils shrink, lungs fill with fluid, the heart goes into spasm.

climax.text: Atropine can counteract sarin if given fast enough. It blocks the excess acetylcholine at receptor sites.

punchline.text: Block the off-switch for nerves. Every muscle fires until death.

quiz.question: How does sarin kill?
options: It blocks the enzyme that stops nerve signals, causing uncontrolled muscle contraction
It prevents the blood from clotting

details.summary: Sarin is an organophosphate nerve agent that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing continuous nerve stimulation that leads to muscle paralysis, seizures, and respiratory failure. It is classified as a weapon of mass destruction and is banned under the Chemical Weapons Convention.
details.whyItMatters: Sarin attacks in Syria and the Tokyo subway demonstrated that nerve agents remain active threats. Understanding their chemistry is critical for emergency medical response and arms control verification.
takeaways: Sarin permanently blocks the enzyme that clears nerve signals
Exposure causes uncontrolled muscle contractions and respiratory failure
Atropine and pralidoxime are the standard emergency antidotes

faq.question: How does sarin cause death so rapidly after exposure?
faq.answer: Sarin prevents acetylcholinesterase from breaking down acetylcholine at nerve junctions. This causes continuous stimulation of muscles, glands, and organs. The diaphragm and airway muscles spasm and eventually paralyze, causing death from suffocation.

faq.question: What is the standard treatment protocol for sarin exposure?
faq.answer: First responders administer atropine to block excess acetylcholine effects and pralidoxime to reactivate inhibited acetylcholinesterase if given quickly. Diazepam controls seizures. Decontamination by removing clothing and washing skin is also critical in the first minutes.
